title: Probability
tagline: Experimental and theoretical probability, sample space, events, and simple compound probability problems.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Probability is the study of the likelihood of events occurring. In ICSE Class X, the focus is on theoretical (classical) probability, where all outcomes are equally likely. The chapter covers the definition of probability as the ratio of favourable outcomes to total equally likely outcomes, the sample space (the set of all possible outcomes), and events (subsets of the sample space). Students learn to calculate probabilities for single experiments (coin toss, die throw, card draw) and simple compound events involving 'and' (intersection) and 'or' (union). The chapter also covers the complementary event: P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

learningOutcomes: Define the sample space of a random experiment and identify the total number of equally likely outcomes.
Calculate the probability of a single event: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.
Calculate the probability of the complementary event: P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
Calculate the probability of simple compound events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B), and P(A and B) for independent events.
Solve probability problems involving coins, dice, cards, and everyday objects.
Distinguish between independent and dependent events (basic understanding).
Express probability as a fraction, decimal, or percentage, and interpret the result.

blocks.text: Probability measures the likelihood that an event will occur. It is expressed as a number between 0 and 1, where 0 means the event is impossible and 1 means the event is certain (sure). The theoretical (classical) definition of probability, which is used in ICSE Class X, assumes that all outcomes of an experiment are equally likely. The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a subset of the sample space — one or more outcomes that we are interested in. The probability of an event E is given by P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (total number of equally likely outcomes). The complementary event 'not E' has probability P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
A Venn diagram or list showing the sample space and events for a coin toss or die throw.

items: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 (inclusive).
P(E) = 1 means the event is certain; P(E) = 0 means the event is impossible.
The complementary event satisfies P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
Theoretical probability assumes all outcomes are equally likely.
The sample space lists all possible outcomes.

learn.Title: Sample Space and Equally Likely Outcomes

blocks.text: The sample space of a random experiment is the set of all possible outcomes. In ICSE Class X, the most common experiments are: (a) tossing a fair coin, with sample space {H, T}; (b) throwing a fair die, with sample space {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}; (c) drawing a card from a well-shuffled deck of 52 playing cards, with 4 suits (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs) and 13 ranks (A, 2, 3, …, 10, J, Q, K) in each suit. Two events are equally likely if they have the same probability of occurring. For a fair coin or fair die, all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely.

items.text: Write the sample space for tossing a coin twice.
items.note: The first toss can be H or T, and the second toss can be H or T, giving 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes.

items.text: Write the sample space for throwing a die and getting a number less than 4.
items.note: The die has 6 faces, all equally likely. Three outcomes (1, 2, 3) are less than 4.

items.text: Write the sample space for drawing a card from a standard deck and getting a queen.
items.note: A standard deck has 52 cards, 4 of which are queens.

items: The sample space for a coin toss is {H, T}; for a die throw, {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
For multiple coins/dice, the sample space is the Cartesian product: e.g., two coins give {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
All outcomes in a sample space for a fair experiment are equally likely.
The total number of outcomes for drawing a card from a 52-card deck is 52.

learn.title: Sample Space of a Random Experiment

blocks.text: The probability of an event E is P(E) = n(E) / n(S), where n(E) is the number of outcomes favourable to E, and n(S) is the total number of outcomes in the sample space S. The probability of the complementary event 'not E' is P(not E) = 1 − P(E). A sure event has probability 1; an impossible event has probability 0. For any event E, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.

items.text: A die is thrown. Find the probability of getting (i) a number greater than 4, (ii) an even number, (iii) a number less than 7.
items.note: The sample space has 6 equally likely outcomes. (i) Two outcomes (5, 6) are greater than 4. (ii) Three outcomes (2, 4, 6) are even. (iii) All six outcomes are less than 7.

items.text: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Find the probability of drawing (i) a king, (ii) a red card, (iii) a king or a red card.
items.note: Use the addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). There are 4 kings and 26 red cards, but 2 cards are both kings and red (king of hearts and king of diamonds).

items.text: A bag contains 5 red balls, 3 blue balls, and 2 green balls. A ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that the ball is (i) red, (ii) not red, (iii) blue or green.
items.note: Total balls = 10. (i) 5 are red. (ii) The complementary event 'not red' has probability 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. (iii) 3 blue + 2 green = 5 favourable outcomes out of 10.

items: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
P(E) = 1 is a sure event; P(E) = 0 is an impossible event.
For compound events, use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Probability is always between 0 and 1 inclusive.

blocks.text: For two events A and B: (a) P(A and B) is the probability that both A and B occur. If A and B are independent (the occurrence of one does not affect the other), then P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). (b) P(A or B) is the probability that at least one of A or B occurs. The general rule is P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). This accounts for the overlap where both A and B occur (otherwise they would be counted twice).

items.text: A die is thrown twice. Find the probability of getting a 6 on the first throw and a 5 on the second throw.
items.note: The two throws are independent events. The outcome of the first does not affect the second. P(6 on first) = 1/6, P(5 on second) = 1/6, so P(both) = 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.

items.text: A die is thrown. Find the probability of getting a number that is either a 3 or an even number.
items.note: The events 'getting a 3' and 'getting an even number' are mutually exclusive (they cannot happen simultaneously), so P(3 and even) = 0, and the addition rule simplifies to P(A) + P(B).

items.text: A bag contains 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
items.note: The draws are without replacement, so the second probability depends on the first. P(first red) = 3/5. Given first red, P(second red) = 2/4 = 1/2. Multiply: 3/5 × 1/2 = 3/10.

items: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events.
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) (general addition rule).
If A and B are mutually exclusive (cannot both happen), then P(A and B) = 0 and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
Without replacement: probabilities change after each draw; with replacement: probabilities stay the same.
Always check whether events are independent, mutually exclusive, or neither.

blocks.text: The complement of an event E, denoted 'not E' or E', is the event that E does not occur. The key relationship is P(not E) = 1 − P(E). This is useful when it is easier to calculate the probability that an event does not happen than that it does. For example, 'at least one' problems are often solved by computing P(none) = 1 − P(none of the desired outcomes).

items.text: A die is thrown. Find the probability of getting at least one 6 in two throws.
items.note: It is easier to compute the probability of the complementary event 'no 6 in two throws'. P(no 6 on one throw) = 5/6. For two independent throws: (5/6)² = 25/36. Then P(at least one 6) = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.

items.text: A box contains 5 defective and 10 non-defective bulbs. Two bulbs are drawn at random. Find the probability that at least one is defective.
items.note: P(first non-defective) = 10/15 = 2/3. Given first non-defective, P(second non-defective) = 9/14. So P(both non-defective) = (2/3) × (9/14) = 18/42 = 3/7. Then P(at least one defective) = 1 − 3/7 = 4/7.

items.text: A factory produces light bulbs. 2% of the bulbs are defective. If a quality inspector randomly selects 3 bulbs, find the probability that at least one is defective.
items.note: P(none defective) = (0.98)³ because the probability of a non-defective bulb is 0.98, and the selections are independent (with replacement or from a large population). P(at least one defective) = 1 − 0.941192 = 0.058808.

items: P(not E) = 1 − P(E) is the key complementary relationship.
Complementary events are useful for 'at least one' problems: compute P(none) and subtract from 1.
If events are drawn without replacement, the probabilities change; if with replacement, they stay the same.
The complementary event 'not E' includes all outcomes in the sample space that are not in E.

learn.Title: Standard Probability Experiments

blocks.text: This section summarises the sample spaces and probabilities for the standard experiments used in ICSE Class X: coin tosses, die throws, and card draws. Students should be able to quickly write the sample space and compute probabilities for any event within it.

blocks.caption: Standard experiments: sample spaces and probabilities

items: Coin: 2 outcomes; two coins: 4 outcomes; three coins: 8 outcomes (2ⁿ).
Die: 6 outcomes; two dice: 36 outcomes (6²).
Card deck: 52 outcomes; jokerless.
Memorise these sample spaces; they are used in most probability problems.
For 'at least one' problems, use the complementary: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

learn.title: Standard Experiments: Coin, Die, and Card

blocks.text: The questions that follow move from defining sample spaces and computing basic probabilities through compound events and complementary events to standard experiment problems. Work each one by identifying the experiment, writing the sample space, and applying the probability formula.

keyPoints: Probability of an event E is P(E) = n(E) / n(S), where n(E) is the number of favourable outcomes and n(S) is the total number of equally likely outcomes.
The probability of an event always lies between 0 and 1, inclusive.
The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment; each element is a sample point.
If all outcomes are equally likely, each outcome has probability 1 / n(S).
For mutually exclusive events A and B, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B); for non-mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
If A and B are independent, P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B); if not independent, P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B given A).
For complementary events, P(not E) = 1 - P(E).
'At least one' problems are often easiest using the complement: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none).
In sampling without replacement, the probabilities change after each draw because the sample space reduces.
Counting outcomes (permutations and combinations) is often needed to find n(E) and n(S) in more complex experiments.
examFocus: Always list or describe the sample space before calculating any probability; most mistakes come from an incomplete sample space.
State whether outcomes are equally likely; the formula P(E) = n(E) / n(S) applies only when they are.
For 'or' questions, check first whether the events are mutually exclusive before adding probabilities.
For 'and' questions with independent events, multiply; for dependent events, condition on the first outcome.
For 'at least one' problems, prefer the complement approach and explain why.
When drawing without replacement, recompute the sample space after each draw and show that step.
For coin, die, and card problems, quote the standard counts: 2, 6, 52, and the suit/face breakdowns that the question depends on.
Express the final probability in simplest fractional form unless the question asks for a decimal.

vocabulary.meaning: A number between 0 and 1 that measures how likely an event is to occur; 0 means impossible and 1 means certain.
An action whose outcome cannot be predicted with certainty in advance, such as tossing a coin or throwing a die.
A single possible result of a random experiment.
The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, often denoted by S.
One element of the sample space; a single outcome.
A subset of the sample space; any collection of outcomes to which a probability can be assigned.
Outcomes that have the same chance of occurring; the basis for the formula P(E) = n(E) / n(S).
Events that cannot occur together; their intersection is empty, so P(A and B) = 0.
Events where the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other; for such events, P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B).
The event that the given event does not occur, denoted not E or E'; P(not E) = 1 - P(E).
Sampling in which each chosen item is not returned, so the sample space reduces after each draw.

questions.prompt: The probability of an event E is given by P(E) = ______, where all outcomes are equally likely.
questions.explanation: When all outcomes are equally likely, the probability of event E is the number of favourable outcomes n(E) divided by the total number of outcomes n(S).

questions.prompt: The probability of an event always lies between ______ and ______, inclusive.
questions.explanation: By definition, probability is a number from 0 (impossible event) to 1 (certain event), inclusive. For any event E, 0 <= P(E) <= 1.

questions.prompt: The probability of an impossible event is ______.
questions.explanation: An impossible event has no favourable outcomes, so n(E) = 0 and P(E) = 0. The probability 0 means the event cannot occur.

questions.prompt: Write the sample space for tossing a fair coin twice.
questions.explanation: Each toss can be Heads (H) or Tails (T). For two tosses the ordered pairs are HH, HT, TH, and TT, so the sample space has 4 equally likely outcomes.

questions.prompt: Write the sample space for throwing a fair six-faced die once.
questions.explanation: A fair six-faced die has six outcomes, numbered 1 through 6, all equally likely. The sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and n(S) = 6.

questions.prompt: A die is thrown once. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is ______.
questions.explanation: The favourable outcomes are 5 and 6, so n(E) = 2. With n(S) = 6, P(E) = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.prompt: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Find the probability that the card is a queen.
questions.explanation: There are 4 queens in a deck of 52 cards, all equally likely. So P(queen) = 4/52 = 1/13.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue, and 2 green balls. One ball is drawn at random. The probability that it is blue is ______.
questions.explanation: Total balls = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10. Blue balls = 3, so P(blue) = 3/10.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. One ball is drawn. Find the probability that it is not red.
questions.explanation: Not red means the ball is blue. Total balls = 8, blue balls = 3, so P(not red) = P(blue) = 3/8.

questions.prompt: For any event E, P(not E) = ______.
questions.explanation: The complement of E is the event that E does not occur. Its probability is P(not E) = 1 - P(E).

questions.prompt: A die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting at least one 6 in two throws.
questions.explanation: It is easier to use the complement. In two throws, total outcomes = 36. The complement is no 6 in either throw, which has 5 * 5 = 25 outcomes. So P(at least one 6) = 1 - 25/36 = 11/36.

questions.prompt: If events A and B are mutually exclusive, then P(A and B) = ______.
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so their intersection is empty and P(A and B) = 0. That is why the answer is 0 (cannot both occur).

questions.prompt: A die is thrown twice. Find the probability of getting a 6 on the first throw and an even number on the second throw.
questions.explanation: The two throws are independent. P(6 on first) = 1/6 and P(even on second) = 3/6 = 1/2, so P(both) = (1/6) * (1/2) = 1/12.

questions.prompt: Two events A and B are independent. Then P(A and B) = ______.
questions.explanation: For independent events, the occurrence of one does not affect the other, so the probability that both occur is the product P(A) * P(B).

questions.prompt: A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
questions.explanation: Total balls = 5. First draw red: 3/5. Without replacement, second draw red: 2/4 = 1/2. So P(both red) = (3/5) * (1/2) = 3/10.

questions.prompt: A die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting (i) a prime number, (ii) a number greater than 2, (iii) a number divisible by 3.
questions.explanation: Sample space has 6 equally likely outcomes. (i) Prime numbers on a die are 2, 3, 5: 3 outcomes, so P = 3/6 = 1/2. (ii) Numbers greater than 2 are 3, 4, 5, 6: 4 outcomes, so P = 4/6 = 2/3. (iii) Numbers divisible by 3 are 3 and 6: 2 outcomes, so P = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.prompt: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Find the probability that the card is (i) a heart, (ii) a king, (iii) a heart or a king, (iv) neither a heart nor a king.
questions.explanation: (i) 13 hearts out of 52 gives P = 13/52 = 1/4. (ii) 4 kings out of 52 gives P = 4/52 = 1/13. (iii) P(heart or king) = P(heart) + P(king) - P(heart and king) = 13/52 + 4/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. (iv) P(neither) = 1 - 4/13 = 9/13.

questions.prompt: A box contains 5 defective and 10 non-defective bulbs. Two bulbs are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that both are non-defective.
questions.explanation: Total bulbs = 15. First non-defective: 10/15 = 2/3. Without replacement, second non-defective: 9/14. So P(both non-defective) = (2/3) * (9/14) = 18/42 = 3/7.

questions.prompt: A factory produces light bulbs and 2% are defective. If three bulbs are selected at random with replacement, find the probability that none is defective.
questions.explanation: With replacement the selections are independent. P(non-defective) = 98% = 0.98. So P(none defective in three) = (0.98)^3 = 0.941192.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 4 white, 5 red, and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that (i) both are red, (ii) one is white and one is blue, (iii) at least one is red.
questions.explanation: Total balls = 4 + 5 + 6 = 15. (i) Both red: first draw red with probability 5/15, then second red with probability 4/14, so P(both red) = (5/15) * (4/14) = 20/210 = 2/21. (ii) One white and one blue occurs in two orders: white then blue, or blue then white. P(white then blue) = (4/15)*(6/14) = 24/210, and P(blue then white) = (6/15)*(4/14) = 24/210, so P(one white and one blue) = 48/210 = 8/35. (iii) At least one red is easiest via the complement: P(no red) = P(first not red and second not red) = (10/15)*(9/14) = 90/210 = 3/7, so P(at least one red) = 1 - 3/7 = 4/7.

questions.prompt: A coin is tossed twice. The probability of getting exactly one head is ______.
questions.explanation: Sample space is {HH, HT, TH, TT}, 4 equally likely outcomes. Exactly one head occurs in HT and TH, 2 outcomes, so P = 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.prompt: Two dice are thrown simultaneously. Find the probability that the sum of the numbers on the two dice is 7.
questions.explanation: Total outcomes = 6 * 6 = 36. Pairs that sum to 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): 6 outcomes. So P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.prompt: A die is thrown. Let A be the event 'getting an even number' and B be the event 'getting a prime number'. Find P(A), P(B), P(A and B), and P(A or B).
questions.explanation: Sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. A = {2, 4, 6} has 3 outcomes: P(A) = 3/6 = 1/2. B = {2, 3, 5} has 3 outcomes: P(B) = 3/6 = 1/2. A and B = {2} has 1 outcome: P(A and B) = 1/6. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) = 1/2 + 1/2 - 1/6 = 5/6.
